screens.title: Custom Message Types and Message Generation
screens.narratorSegment: In robotics we often need messages that match the problem domain. This lesson shows how a simple text blueprint, a. msg file, becomes the single source of truth that ROS compiles into language-specific message types. You will learn why defining messages in. msg files matters, how the build system turns those declarations into Python classes and C++ structs, and how to avoid the common pitfalls that stop imports from working. We’ll walk through an example RobotStatus message, the package. xml and CMakeLists. txt settings required to enable message generation, and the steps you must run after building so your shell finds the generated modules. I’ll also show practical CLI habits — roscd for jumping to a package and tab completion to save time and reduce errors. By the end, you should be able to design a small SensorData message, update your package to generate it, and run a publisher and subscriber to validate the flow. Think now about a single message your robot needs and how you would express its fields.

keyIdea.title: Why .msg files matter
keyIdea.text: A .msg file declares the exact structure used by all nodes. ROS generates serialization and language bindings so different nodes can exchange well-defined data reliably.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.3 › Overview

Custom Message Types & Message Generation

Blueprint your robot's data structures using .msg files, compile them into Python and C++ types, and learn CLI habits to verify generated modules.

In this lesson
Create .msg blueprints, configure building, import generated types in Python and C++, and use roscd and tab completion to speed development.
.msg Blueprints
Fields list the structure used to generate code.
Build Factory
CMake and catkin_make produce Python classes and C++ headers.
Verify & Use
Source setup.bash, import the generated module, and run publisher/subscriber tests.
Explore key topics
Designing a .msg
List types and names. Use package-qualified names for nested messages.
CMake & Generation
Add message_generation, declare add_message_files, and call generate_messages.
Debugging imports
Common fixes: add dependencies, catkin_make, source setup.bash.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These objectives map to practical skills you need when creating and using custom ROS messages. First, you will learn how to author. msg files that describe message fields clearly and correctly so the build system can generate types in multiple languages. Second, you will configure package. xml and CMakeLists. txt to include message_generation and message_runtime so catkin_make produces usable Python and C++ bindings. Third, you will run catkin_make, source the workspace, and import and use the generated types in publisher and subscriber nodes. Finally, you will use shell conveniences—roscd and tab completion—to navigate packages and avoid typing mistakes. Each objective pairs a definition with a hands-on habit: author the message, declare the build steps, run the build and source, and verify with an example publisher/subscriber. These skills matter because they turn a design into working inter-process communication that is language-neutral. Consider which objective feels most unfamiliar now; we will practice them all with examples and a small lab.

screens.title: What is a custom .msg file?
screens.narratorSegment: A. msg file in ROS is a compact, language-neutral blueprint that lists each field of a message with its type and name. Defining messages this way gives ROS the information needed to generate serialization code, Python classes, and C++ headers automatically. For example, the RobotStatus. msg blueprint lists a string robot_name, an integer battery_percent, a float temperature, a boolean is_moving, and a geometry_msgs/Pose called current_pose. That Pose field demonstrates nesting: a custom message can include standard or other custom messages as fields, creating structured, recursive data without extra effort. A concrete example: if you are building a fleet management node, a RobotStatus message can be published by each robot to a fleet monitor; the monitor receives typed fields it can depend on for dashboard displays and decision logic. A common misconception is to think you can use direct language structures like Python dicts and expect the system to share them across languages. That does not work because ROS needs a single schema to generate wire-level serialization. Key takeaway: the. msg file is the authoritative schema for inter-node communication. What fields would your robot need to include in its status message?

keyIdea.title: .msg = authoritative schema
keyIdea.text: The .msg file defines the structure once so ROS can generate consistent code and serialization for all supported languages.

content.html:
Definition

.msg file

A plain text file listing typed fields. It is the single source of truth ROS uses to generate message code for different languages.

Why it matters
  • Ensures consistent serialization across nodes and languages.
  • Enables code generation for Python classes and C++ headers.
  • Supports nested messages for complex structures.
Analogy
Think of the .msg as a data contract: every publisher and subscriber agrees on the field names and types before exchanging values.
Example blueprint
# File: msg/RobotStatus.msg
string robot_name
int32 battery_percent
float32 temperature
bool is_moving
geometry_msgs/Pose current_pose
Concrete use case

A robot publishes RobotStatus periodically. A monitoring node receives typed fields and displays battery, temperature, and pose on a dashboard for operator decisions.

Key Takeaway

Define message fields in .msg files so ROS can generate consistent types and serialization across languages.

Common mistake
Using language-specific structures instead of .msg files prevents automatic generation and cross-language communication.
Check your understanding
Name three fields your robot status needs and explain why each type is appropriate.

screens.title: CMakeLists and package.xml changes
screens.narratorSegment: To generate Python and C++ bindings you must tell catkin what to produce. In package. xml, add a build dependency on message_generation and an exec dependency on message_runtime so the build and run-time pieces are declared. In CMakeLists. txt you must find the message generation package and list the message files using add_message_files, then call generate_messages with any dependent packages the messages reference. For example, if your. msg references geometry_msgs or std_msgs, include them under DEPENDENCIES when calling generate_messages. Also ensure catkin_package lists message_runtime under CATKIN_DEPENDS. A concrete sequence: add the two tags to package. xml, add message_generation to find_package, add_message_files(FILE RobotStatus. msg), generate_messages(DEPENDENCIES std_msgs geometry_msgs), and catkin_package(CATKIN_DEPENDS message_runtime). A common mistake is adding dependencies only to package. xml but not calling add_message_files in CMakeLists, which leaves no input for the generator. The takeaway is that both package metadata and CMake instructions must match the messages you define, otherwise generation will silently be skipped or fail. CMakeLists and package.xml changes means both package.xml and cmakelists.txt must declare message build and runtime dependencies and list the message files for generation.. In practical terms, enable message generation with the right dependencies and declarations. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Two-sided configuration
keyIdea.text: Both package.xml and CMakeLists.txt must declare message build and runtime dependencies and list the message files for generation.

content.html:
package.xml
<build_depend>message_generation</build_depend>
<exec_depend>message_runtime</exec_depend>
These entries tell the build and runtime systems about message generation support. Forgetting them often causes missing module errors after build.
CMakeLists.txt (essential parts)
find_package(catkin REQUIRED COMPONENTS
  roscpp
  rospy
  std_msgs
  geometry_msgs
  message_generation
)

add_message_files(
  FILES
  RobotStatus.msg
)

generate_messages(
  DEPENDENCIES
  std_msgs
  geometry_msgs
)

catkin_package(
  CATKIN_DEPENDS message_runtime
)
Ensure listed components match the types your messages reference. Mismatched dependencies cause compile-time errors or missing generated outputs.
Pro tip
Keep message file names in add_message_files in sync with msg/ directory entries to avoid missing inputs during generation.
Common mistake
Omitting message_generation in find_package but adding package.xml entries will not produce code without CMake declarations.
Key Takeaway

Add both build and runtime dependencies and declare message files in CMake so generate_messages produces usable types.

screens.title: Build, Source, and Verify
screens.narratorSegment: After you declare message files and dependencies, the build step produces the language bindings. The usual sequence is to change to your workspace root, run catkin_make, and after a successful build run source devel/setup. bash so your current shell session picks up the generated modules and updated PYTHONPATH. A concrete example: cd to ~/catkin_ws, run catkin_make, then source devel/setup. bash. If you skip sourcing, Python will not find the generated package module and imports will raise ImportError. Verification steps include running a small Python REPL and attempting from my_first_robot. msg import RobotStatus or checking the devel/lib and devel/include directories for generated outputs. Another useful check is rospack find my_first_robot to confirm the package path. A common misconception is that a successful build always implies immediate availability; builds only place files on disk—sourcing updates your environment. Summary: build, then source, then verify imports in the language you plan to use. Build, Source, and Verify means catkin_make writes generated code to devel; sourcing setup.bash updates your shell so language runtimes can find the new modules.. In practical terms, turn message blueprints into usable code and make them visible to your shell. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Build then source
keyIdea.text: catkin_make writes generated code to devel; sourcing setup.bash updates your shell so language runtimes can find the new modules.

content.html:
Step-by-step
  1. cd ~/catkin_ws
  2. catkin_make
  3. source devel/setup.bash
  4. python -c "from my_first_robot.msg import RobotStatus" to verify
Run these every time you rebuild generated messages, or add the source command to your shell startup during development.
Terminal checks
# Build and source
cd ~/catkin_ws
catkin_make
source devel/setup.bash

# Quick Python import check
python -c "from my_first_robot.msg import RobotStatus; print('ok')"
If import fails, re-check CMakeLists and package.xml and ensure you sourced the workspace that contains the generated code.
Troubleshoot
Use rospack find and roscd to confirm package locations and that devel/setup.bash belongs to the workspace you built.
Misconception
A successful catkin_make does not alter your current shell until you source the new setup file. Missing source is the leading cause of import errors.
Key Takeaway

Always source the workspace after building so generated message modules are visible to Python and other tools.

screens.title: Importing and using custom messages in Python
screens.narratorSegment: Once generation and sourcing are complete, Python code can import the generated class and use it like any other class. The typical pattern is from my_first_robot. msg import RobotStatus, then instantiate status = RobotStatus(). You set fields directly: status. robot_name = 'TurtleBot_01', status. battery_percent = 85, and so on. Nested fields such as current_pose. position. x are available because the generator includes standard message types intact. A concrete publisher node publishes at a fixed rate, setting simulated values each loop. When designing publishers, ensure that field types match the. msg declaration; assigning a string to an int field will raise an error. A common beginner mistake is to forget to import the package-specific module name; using from msg import RobotStatus without the package name will fail. After publishing, verify messages with rostopic echo to inspect the fields as they flow across ROS. Practice: write a small publisher that sends RobotStatus at 1 Hz with changing battery percent and confirm reception in a subscriber. Importing and using custom messages in Python means import the generated class, instantiate it, assign fields directly—including nested fields—and publish like any standard message type.. In practical terms, create instances, set fields, and publish messages. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Python usage
keyIdea.text: Import the generated class, instantiate it, assign fields directly—including nested fields—and publish like any standard message type.

content.html:
Example Python snippet
from my_first_robot.msg import RobotStatus

status = RobotStatus()
status.robot_name = "TurtleBot_01"
status.battery_percent = 85
status.temperature = 42.5
status.is_moving = True
status.current_pose.position.x = 1.0
status.current_pose.position.y = 2.0

# In a publisher loop: pub.publish(status)
Note how nested fields are accessed via dot notation. This mirrors standard Python object usage and keeps code readable.
Concrete example
A sensor node publishes RobotStatus with battery percent decreasing over time; a monitor node subscribes and alerts when battery drops below a threshold.
Common mistake
Using the wrong import path or failing to source the workspace causes ImportError before you run any code logic.
Key Takeaway

After generation and sourcing import the package.msg module and assign fields directly. Use rostopic echo to inspect messages at runtime.

screens.title: Using generated messages in C++
screens.narratorSegment: In C++ the generator creates headers corresponding to each message. To use RobotStatus, include in your node and create an instance: my_first_robot::RobotStatus status. Field assignments are similar: status. robot_name = "TurtleBot_01" and status. battery_percent = 85. Nested messages are available as members, so you can set status. current_pose. position. x = 1.0. C++ code must also link against the generated message libraries; ensure your CMakeLists adds appropriate targets that depend on ${catkin_LIBRARIES} and that generate_messages was executed during the build. A common mismatch arises when the C++ include path doesn’t point to devel/include because the workspace wasn’t sourced or the build failed. Another common pitfall is forgetting to add message_runtime to catkin_package; that prevents the consumer from finding the runtime dependency. After compiling, run your C++ publisher and inspect messages with rostopic echo just as you would for Python. Practice writing a tiny node that publishes RobotStatus and ensure headers and linking are correct. Using generated messages in C++ means include the generated header, create the namespaced struct, set fields directly, and ensure the build links message libraries correctly.. In practical terms, include headers and set fields on generated structs. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: C++ usage
keyIdea.text: Include the generated header, create the namespaced struct, set fields directly, and ensure the build links message libraries correctly.

content.html:
Example C++ snippet
#include <my_first_robot/RobotStatus.h>

my_first_robot::RobotStatus status;
status.robot_name = "TurtleBot_01";
status.battery_percent = 85;
status.temperature = 42.5;
status.is_moving = true;
status.current_pose.position.x = 1.0;
status.current_pose.position.y = 2.0;

// publisher->publish(status);
Remember to add message_runtime and link targets in CMakeLists for successful compilation and linking against generated message libraries.
Build note
If you add a C++ node, ensure target_link_libraries includes ${catkin_LIBRARIES} so message types resolve at link time.
Misconception
Assuming C++ can find headers without sourcing the workspace can lead to compile-time include errors. Build and source accordingly.
Key Takeaway

In C++ include the generated header and set fields on the namespaced struct; ensure CMake links to generated message libraries.

screens.title: .msg vs .srv vs .action
screens.narratorSegment: ROS uses three file types to define communication interfaces. A. msg file defines the data carried by topics for publish-subscribe patterns, suitable for streaming state or sensor data. A. srv file defines a request and response pair for synchronous client-server interactions where one node requests work and another replies. An. action file describes a goal, feedback, and result pattern for long-running tasks that need preemption and progress updates. In this chapter we focus on. msg because it describes the payload for publishers and subscribers. A common confusion is to try to use a topic for request-reply semantics; while you can emulate it, using services provides clear synchronous semantics and built-in request/response structure. For example, use. msg to stream SensorData at 1 Hz, use. srv when you need a node to perform a discrete computation immediately, and use. action for lengthy navigation goals that provide continuous feedback. Choosing the right file type simplifies node design and prevents misusing topics for requests that should be services. .msg vs .srv vs .action means .msg for streaming data, .srv for synchronous requests, .action for long-running goals with feedback.. In practical terms, different file types for different communication patterns. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Common mistakes and fixes
screens.narratorSegment: Several recurring mistakes block new ROS developers when working with custom messages. First, forgetting to add message_generation or message_runtime to the package files is the leading cause of ImportError when trying to import the generated module. The fix is to add build_depend message_generation and exec_depend message_runtime to package. xml and ensure CMakeLists calls add_message_files and generate_messages. Second, not sourcing devel/setup. bash after catkin_make leaves Python unaware of the generated package. The fix is to source the correct workspace or add the source to your active shell profile while developing. Third, using relative message names in. msg files can break nested references; always qualify messages from other packages as other_package/MyOtherMsg. Fourth, naming conflicts occur when two packages define messages with identical names; avoid duplicate message names across packages or use package-qualified names to disambiguate. For each problem, I recommend a verification step: re-check package. xml and CMakeLists, rebuild, source, and then attempt a python import or rospack find. These disciplined checks quickly reveal the cause and keep development moving. In robotics we often need messages that match the problem domain. This lesson shows how a simple text blueprint, a. msg file, becomes the single source of truth that ROS compiles into language-specific message types. You will learn why defining messages in. msg files matters, how the build system turns those declarations into Python classes and C++ structs, and how to avoid the common pitfalls that stop imports from working. We’ll walk through an example RobotStatus message, the package. xml and CMakeLists. txt settings required to enable message generation, and the steps you must run after building so your shell finds the generated modules. I’ll also show practical CLI habits — roscd for jumping to a package and tab completion to save time and reduce errors. By the end, you should be able to design a small SensorData message, update your package to generate it, and run a publisher and subscriber to validate the flow. Think now about a single message your robot needs and how you would express its fields.

These objectives map to practical skills you need when creating and using custom ROS messages. First, you will learn how to author. msg files that describe message fields clearly and correctly so the build system can generate types in multiple languages. Second, you will configure package. xml and CMakeLists. txt to include message_generation and message_runtime so catkin_make produces usable Python and C++ bindings. Third, you will run catkin_make, source the workspace, and import and use the generated types in publisher and subscriber nodes. Finally, you will use shell conveniences—roscd and tab completion—to navigate packages and avoid typing mistakes. Each objective pairs a definition with a hands-on habit: author the message, declare the build steps, run the build and source, and verify with an example publisher/subscriber. These skills matter because they turn a design into working inter-process communication that is language-neutral. Consider which objective feels most unfamiliar now; we will practice them all with examples and a small lab.

This second objectives slide links each learning goal to a hands-on step so you can practice confidently. You will create a SensorData. msg file with typed fields and place it in msg/ so catkin knows where to find it. You will edit package. xml to declare message_generation and message_runtime, and you will modify CMakeLists. txt to call add_message_files and generate_messages so the factory produces outputs. After a build, you will run catkin_make, then source devel/setup. bash to update your Python path and include directories. You will write small publisher and subscriber nodes to send and receive the custom message and check results with rostopic echo. Finally, you will use roscd to move to your package folder quickly and use tab completion to avoid errors when calling rosrun or referencing topics. Practice each step deliberately, verify imports after sourcing, and note how a missing dependency or unsourced environment leads to import failures.

A. msg file in ROS is a compact, language-neutral blueprint that lists each field of a message with its type and name. Defining messages this way gives ROS the information needed to generate serialization code, Python classes, and C++ headers automatically. For example, the RobotStatus. msg blueprint lists a string robot_name, an integer battery_percent, a float temperature, a boolean is_moving, and a geometry_msgs/Pose called current_pose. That Pose field demonstrates nesting: a custom message can include standard or other custom messages as fields, creating structured, recursive data without extra effort. A concrete example: if you are building a fleet management node, a RobotStatus message can be published by each robot to a fleet monitor; the monitor receives typed fields it can depend on for dashboard displays and decision logic. A common misconception is to think you can use direct language structures like Python dicts and expect the system to share them across languages. That does not work because ROS needs a single schema to generate wire-level serialization. Key takeaway: the. msg file is the authoritative schema for inter-node communication. What fields would your robot need to include in its status message?

To generate Python and C++ bindings you must tell catkin what to produce. In package. xml, add a build dependency on message_generation and an exec dependency on message_runtime so the build and run-time pieces are declared. In CMakeLists. txt you must find the message generation package and list the message files using add_message_files, then call generate_messages with any dependent packages the messages reference. For example, if your. msg references geometry_msgs or std_msgs, include them under DEPENDENCIES when calling generate_messages. Also ensure catkin_package lists message_runtime under CATKIN_DEPENDS. A concrete sequence: add the two tags to package. xml, add message_generation to find_package, add_message_files(FILE RobotStatus. msg), generate_messages(DEPENDENCIES std_msgs geometry_msgs), and catkin_package(CATKIN_DEPENDS message_runtime). A common mistake is adding dependencies only to package. xml but not calling add_message_files in CMakeLists, which leaves no input for the generator. The takeaway is that both package metadata and CMake instructions must match the messages you define, otherwise generation will silently be skipped or fail. CMakeLists and package.xml changes means both package.xml and cmakelists.txt must declare message build and runtime dependencies and list the message files for generation.. In practical terms, enable message generation with the right dependencies and declarations. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

After you declare message files and dependencies, the build step produces the language bindings. The usual sequence is to change to your workspace root, run catkin_make, and after a successful build run source devel/setup. bash so your current shell session picks up the generated modules and updated PYTHONPATH.
